text: Before you can reason about why training is slow, or plan capacity for a new job, you need to be able to look at a topology diagram and know what each layer means. This lesson teaches you to read solara-train's topology the way the platform team does.

There are three layers, and the bandwidth drops by roughly an order of magnitude at each one. Inside a node, all eight H100s connect over NVLink, up to nine hundred gigabytes per second between any two of them. Between nodes, each GPU has its own InfiniBand NDR adapter running at four hundred gigabits per second — call it fifty gigabytes per second, noticeably less than NVLink. And then there's the fabric shape itself — how those adapters wire into switches — which is called rail-optimized.

You can see the intra-node layer directly with a command from GPU Computing: nvidia-smi topo dash m. It prints a matrix where each cell shows the connection between two GPUs — NV18 means an eighteen-link NVLink connection. If you ever see something slower where you expected NV18, that's a sign the node is misconfigured.

Rail-optimized means every GPU with the same index, across every node, shares its own dedicated switch — GPU zero on every node connects to rail zero's switch, GPU one to rail one's, and so on. That matters because NCCL's ring and tree algorithms move data between the same GPU index on different nodes constantly, so giving that traffic its own uncontended switch keeps it from competing with everything else moving across the fabric.

Read any topology in layers — fastest path, bottleneck path, blast radius of a failure, and whether anything's oversubscribed. Those four questions work on any vendor's diagram, not just solara-train's. Up next, lesson five: capacity planning, putting real numbers on GPU-hours and wall-clock time.
